quotes.text: For Unbreakable, Backstreet Boys moved away from the Max Martin–driven sound of their early hits, instead collaborating with a variety of producers to craft a more mature, adult vocal-group style.

Musically, the band described Unbreakable as 'a little bit of old and new,' with the album blending adult contemporary and contemporary pop, incorporating interwoven choral harmonies, piano, strings, guitar, and drums.
The album received mixed reviews from critics, with praise for its polished harmonies, mature and radio-friendly pop sound, while others criticized it for a lack of standout songs and innovation.

It was also their first album without the involvement of longtime collaborators Max Martin and Kristian Lundin, who had worked on all of the group's previous albums, with Dan Muckala assuming a larger role in the album's production.
Out of those 12 songs, 7 of them were written by Max Martin, 4 of which were official singles and were very successful otherwise.
Millennium is extremely consistent all throughout as there are no bad songs here.
The emotion the Backstreet Boys pour in their songs are certainly one of their strong points and this song does a solid job of that.
One thing the Backstreet Boys are known for are their hits and they have absolutely plenty.
Their pitch-perfect harmonies and ability to craft an infectious dance beat have made them a household name, and even a popular internet meme.
Though their sound has always been a staple of the pop genre, whether it was in the '90s or today.
Even with their sound changing as the years went on, there is still something undeniably unique to the Backstreet Boys and their albums.

Unbreakable shows the band trying to find their footing as a newly formed quartet. This album is also the first without producer Max Martin, who is known for creating major hits for other artists such as NSYNC and Britney Spears.

This album isn't a different sound for the boys, but something familiar that was updated for the times. Trying to find who you are as a band minus one member can be a challenge, and this album proves that.
This Is Us has the most unmistakable pop sound in the Backstreet Boys' discography. Big-name artists collaborated on this project, such as Ne-Yo, Pitbull, T-Pain, and former producer Max Martin.
This album does a great job at giving each member solo moments that highlight their vocal range and abilities, more so than on previous albums.
Pop music is constantly evolving, and I believe that the Backstreet Boys evolved with the times on this record.
DNA is the Backstreet Boys' most recent album... It has a new and unique experimental sound that also features their most risqué lyrics to date, featured in songs like 'Passionate.'

By far their most modern sound, DNA shows the band taking more chances with their sound and not shying away from trying something new. The risk paid off, with the album debuting at number one in the US and being generally well-received.

It shows that the Backstreet Boys aren't afraid to switch things up and give fans a surprise or two. They have switched up their sound before, showcasing that it is possible to go from one style to another.
Perhaps one of the most innovative ways to start an album, Black & Blue kicks off with a jarring phone ring as 'The Call' begins to play.

This album starts out strong with the party tracks bringing the listener in, then slowing it down with love ballads at the end. For a turn-of-the-century album, Black & Blue gave the band a great starting point and a fresh new sound that still utilized some of their older tactics.
